DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Feasibility Study, Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection (Thornbury)

## What the study proposes

The study proposes a single, uniform weekly food waste service for all 52,000 households from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households. It projects about 3,290 tonnes a year, treated at Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant. The disposal saving is put at £243,000 against costs of £733,400, giving a net cost of about £490,000. The study says the provisional £520,000 new-burdens allocation would cover this in full.

**Arithmetic.**
- The cost table adds up: £990,000 ÷ 7 = £141,400, and 12 operatives × £34,000 = £408,000.
- The pilot participation rates are correct (66%, 21%, 57%).
- 52,000 × 64% × 1.9 kg × 52 weeks does give about 3,290 tonnes, and £74 × 3,290 ≈ £243,000.

However, three of the study's central conclusions contradict its own figures:
- that flats participated at a similar rate to houses,
- that 64% is the pilot's participation rate, and
- that treatment is covered locally.

## 1. Participation in flats was a third of the rate in houses

Section 2 says participation was "broadly similar across housing types." Table 1 shows **66% for houses and 21% for flats**. Flats participated at about a third of the rate of houses and produced less food waste per participating household (1.4 kg against 1.9 kg).

That is the opposite of the conclusion drawn from it. The case for a single uniform service across the district, which appears in the study's recommendation and in the author's summary, depends on this sentence, and the data don't support it.

Low participation in flats is a common problem. It usually needs a different service design, such as communal food bins, different containers or targeted communication. With about 10,400 flats in the district, a separate approach for them should be costed.

## 2. The projection uses a participation rate that doesn't appear in the pilot

Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate." The pilot's overall rate was **57%**, and 64% appears nowhere in Table 1. The pilot's housing mix (20% flats) matches the district's, so 57% transfers directly.

| Basis | Annual tonnage |
|---|---|
| As stated (64% participation, 1.9 kg) | about 3,290 t |
| By housing type (houses 66% at 1.9 kg; flats 21% at 1.4 kg) | **about 2,870 t** |

Two further cautions about using the pilot as a forecast:
- **It may be optimistic.** Participation in new services often falls once the initial interest wears off.
- **It covers only January to June.** Food waste tonnage varies through the year, so six months is a weak basis for a full-year figure.

## 3. Brookfield cannot take the projected tonnage

Brookfield has confirmed **1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**.

| Projection | Tonnage that must go elsewhere |
|---|---|
| Study's figure (3,290 t) | about 1,490 t a year |
| Corrected figure (2,870 t) | about 1,070 t a year |

The next AD plant is **46 miles away**. The study gives no gate fee, haulage cost or extra vehicle and crew time for that plant.

Sending the excess back to incineration is unlikely to be an option. Separately collected food waste is generally required to go to recycling, such as AD, not to incineration. That point should be confirmed with legal colleagues.

So the statement that "treatment is local" applies to well under two-thirds of the tonnage.

## 4. The service isn't fully funded on the study's own figures

Correcting the tonnage alone removes the margin:
- **Saving at 2,870 t:** £74 × 2,870 ≈ £212,000.
- **Net cost:** £733,400 − £212,000 ≈ **£521,000**.
- That is already slightly more than the £520,000 allocation, *before* any of the additional costs below.

**Additional costs not included:**

| Item | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Haulage and gate fee for the roughly 1,070 t that must go to the 46-mile plant | Treatment for the excess tonnage is not costed |
| Crew on-costs | If £34,000 is salary only, employer pension and National Insurance (NI) usually add about a quarter or more |
| Cover for holidays and sickness | Six crews running every week need relief drivers and loaders |
| Supervision and management | Not costed |
| Phone line and web page | The dedicated line in Section 6 has no cost attached |
| Vehicle financing | Depreciation is shown, but borrowing costs are not |
| Replacement caddies | Not mentioned |

So the author's claim that "every cost line is shown" is not accurate.

Two funding risks also need stating:
- **The allocation is provisional.** The Government has "indicated" that funding will be provided.
- **The vehicles must be ordered in December 2026.** The study should say whether funding will be confirmed by then, and whether new-burdens funding is guaranteed beyond the first year or two.

## 5. Other points

- **The 81% satisfaction figure** comes from "surveyed pilot households." The response rate isn't given, and satisfied participants may be more likely to reply.
- **Statutory deadline.** Section 1 says councils are required to introduce the service but gives no date. My understanding is that the deadline for most councils in England was 31 March 2026, with later dates for councils that have existing contracts. Please check which applies to Thornbury and state it. An April 2027 start may need explaining.
- **Timetable.** The timetable leaves very little room for slippage:
  - Vehicles arrive in March, one month before collections start.
  - Crews are recruited from February, and qualified heavy goods vehicle (HGV) drivers can take time to recruit.
  - No contingency is described if vehicle delivery or recruitment slips.
- **Number of vehicles.** Six vehicles serving 52,000 households a week, including village rounds and trips to a plant 46 miles away for part of the tonnage, should be checked against round modelling.
- **Pilot wards.** The wards were chosen deliberately rather than at random. The study should say how typical they are of the district.

## Suggested revisions

1. Correct Section 2 to say that participation in flats was markedly lower, and cost a separate approach for flats.
2. Base the projection on 57%, or on the rates for each housing type (about 2,870 t), and give a range that allows for participation falling over time.
3. Set out treatment arrangements for the tonnage above Brookfield's 1,800 t limit, including haulage and gate fees, until the plant expands in 2029.
4. Rebuild the cost table to include on-costs, relief staff, supervision, the phone line, financing and the cost of using the second treatment plant. Show the funding gap or surplus honestly.
5. Make the vehicle order conditional on confirmed funding, or state the risk explicitly.
6. State the statutory deadline that applies to Thornbury, and add timetable contingency.

The pilot itself is useful. Participation and contamination in houses look good. But as written, the study's three main conclusions (a uniform service, local treatment, and full funding) are each contradicted by its own figures. Cabinet should see a corrected version before authorising the vehicle order.
